records.name: John Hawkins
records.scaleNote: Led England's first known slaving voyages (1562–68); the first voyage alone took c. 300 Africans from the Sierra Leone coast for sale in Spanish Hispaniola, and he made three to four such voyages in all.
records.origins: Son of William Hawkins, a Plymouth merchant who had traded with the Guinea coast and Brazil. He learned of the profits of selling captives to Spanish colonists through contacts in the Canary Islands.
records.role_summary: Organised the first English slaving expeditions, seizing and buying Africans in Upper Guinea and selling them in the Spanish Caribbean in defiance of Spain's monopoly. His later voyages were backed by London investors and by Elizabeth I, who lent royal ships.

roleDetail.d: Sailed with three ships (Salomon, Swallow, Jonas) to the Sierra Leone coast, took c. 300 captives and sold them in Hispaniola.
For the 1564 voyage Elizabeth I lent the 700-ton royal ship Jesus of Lübeck, making the Crown an investor in the trade.

roleDetail.t: Defeat at San Juan de Ulúa, 1568.
roleDetail.d: His third voyage ended when a Spanish fleet attacked his ships in the Mexican harbour; most ships and many men were lost.

records.legacy: Hawkins became Treasurer of the Navy and a commander against the Spanish Armada in 1588, and was knighted. His coat of arms featured a bound African captive. His voyages are now remembered as the beginning of England's involvement in the transatlantic slave trade.

legacyDetail.d: After 1568 England's slave trade lapsed for nearly a century; Hawkins's later fame rested on reforming the navy.
Since 2020 places named after Hawkins in Plymouth have faced calls for renaming or contextualisation.

records.name: Francis Drake
records.scaleNote: Took part in Hawkins's slaving voyages of the 1560s, captaining the 50-ton Judith on the 1567–68 expedition; he did not run slaving ventures of his own.
records.origins: A Devon-born relative of the Hawkins family, he went to sea young and joined the Hawkins family's Atlantic ventures in the 1560s.
records.role_summary: Served on Hawkins's slaving voyages to West Africa and the Spanish Caribbean, commanding the Judith in 1567–68. He escaped the 1568 Spanish attack at San Juan de Ulúa, an event that shaped his later privateering against Spain.

roleDetail.d: Commanded the smallest ship of Hawkins's third slaving fleet, which raided and traded for captives on the Upper Guinea coast.
One of the few ships to escape the Spanish attack; the episode fuelled his raids on Spanish shipping.

records.legacy: Drake became famous for circumnavigating the globe (1577–80) and fighting the Armada. His early involvement in the slave trade is far less commemorated than his naval exploits, and his statues have been questioned since 2020.

legacyDetail.d: National narratives long presented Drake as a hero while omitting his slaving voyages.

sources.label: World History Encyclopedia — John Hawkins
Encyclopedia.com — Hawkins, John

records.name: Elizabeth I of England
records.scaleNote: Invested in Hawkins's slaving voyages by lending royal ships, including the Jesus of Lübeck (1564, 1567); England's trade remained small until the 1660s.
records.origins: Queen of England from 1558. Her government sought ways to break into Iberian Atlantic commerce without open war with Spain.
records.role_summary: Became a shareholder in John Hawkins's slaving expeditions by contributing royal ships. Although reported to have earlier called such trade 'detestable', she backed the voyages for their profits.

roleDetail.d: Lent the Jesus of Lübeck to Hawkins's second voyage (1564) and to the third (1567).
Established a pattern of Crown backing for slaving later formalised in royal charters under the Stuarts.

records.legacy: Her backing made the English Crown a participant in the trade from its start. The Stuart monarchy later chartered the Royal Adventurers (1660) and the Royal African Company (1672).

legacyDetail.d: Later Stuart monarchs went further, granting monopolies and holding shares in slaving companies.

sources.label: Encyclopedia.com — Hawkins, John
Wikipedia — Jesus of Lübeck

records.name: James, Duke of York (James II)
records.scaleNote: Governor and largest shareholder of the Royal African Company, which shipped more Africans than any other single institution in the trade; many captives were branded 'DY' for him.
records.origins: Younger brother of Charles II and Lord High Admiral after the 1660 Restoration. He led the royal circle that founded chartered companies to break Dutch dominance of West African trade.
records.role_summary: Headed the Company of Royal Adventurers into Africa and then the Royal African Company as governor. Captives shipped by the company were branded with 'DY' (Duke of York) or 'RAC'.

roleDetail.d: He was the company's governor and largest shareholder, keeping the post after becoming king in 1685.
Smithsonian records note many enslaved people were branded with 'DY'; others were marked 'RAC'.
English attacks on Dutch Gold Coast forts in 1664 (including Cape Coast) were part of the Royal Adventurers' war for the trade.

records.legacy: Deposed in 1688, after which Parliament opened the trade (1698). New York is named after him. His role is central to recent debates about the British monarchy's historic links to slavery.

legacyDetail.d: His RAC role is regularly cited in calls for the Royal Family to acknowledge its historic links to slavery.

sources.label: Smithsonian Transcription Center — Stock share certificate for the Royal African Company
Pepys Diary Encyclopedia — Royal African Company
Wikipedia — Royal African Company

records.name: Royal African Company
records.scaleNote: Per SlaveVoyages data cited by historian William Pettigrew, c. 187,700 Africans were carried on 653 company voyages (1672–1731), of whom c. 38,500 died at sea; Pettigrew argues it shipped more captives than any other single institution.
records.origins: Chartered in 1672 by Charles II as successor to the failed Company of Royal Adventurers into Africa, with a monopoly on English trade along the West African coast. Royal family members, courtiers and London merchants were its shareholders.
records.role_summary: Bought captives from African rulers and merchants at forts such as Cape Coast Castle and shipped them to Barbados, Jamaica and other English colonies, branding many with 'DY' or 'RAC'. It also traded gold, ivory and other goods.

roleDetail.d: Held a legal monopoly of English trade to West Africa from 1672 until Parliament opened the trade in 1698 (with a 10% duty on private traders until 1712).
Ran Cape Coast Castle as its Gold Coast headquarters and also held Bunce Island and James Island (Gambia).
Many captives were branded 'DY' for the Duke of York or 'RAC' on the chest.

records.legacy: Weakened by private competition after 1698, the company effectively stopped trading in the 1720s and was replaced in 1750–52 by the Company of Merchants Trading to Africa. Its records survive at The National Archives; its leaders' names, notably Colston's, remain contested in Bristol and London.

legacyDetail.d: The end of the monopoly let thousands of private merchants from London, Bristol and Liverpool enter the trade, greatly increasing British volumes.
Its forts passed to the Company of Merchants Trading to Africa, which ran them until 1821.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Royal African Company
Smithsonian Transcription Center — Stock share certificate for the Royal African Company
Schools History — Lifting of the Royal African Company monopoly

records.name: Edward Colston
records.scaleNote: During his Royal African Company involvement (1680–92) the company is commonly estimated to have transported c. 80,000 Africans; the figure is an estimate and varies by source.
records.origins: Born in Bristol to a merchant family, he made his fortune as a London merchant trading to Spain, Portugal and the Mediterranean. He joined the Royal African Company in 1680.
records.role_summary: Held shares in the Royal African Company and sat on its governing court, serving as deputy governor in 1689–90. His wealth funded schools, almshouses and churches in Bristol, which commemorated him for three centuries.

roleDetail.d: Member of the RAC's Court of Assistants and its deputy governor (1689–90).
Endowed Bristol schools and almshouses; the 1895 statue presented him as a benefactor without mentioning slavery.

records.legacy: On 7 June 2020 Black Lives Matter protesters toppled his statue and pushed it into Bristol Harbour; it is now displayed, graffitied, at the M Shed museum. Colston Hall was renamed Bristol Beacon in 2020, and other Bristol institutions dropped his name.

legacyDetail.d: Four people charged with criminal damage were acquitted by a jury in January 2022.
Colston Hall became Bristol Beacon (announced 23 September 2020) after a campaign begun in 2017.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Statue of Edward Colston

Al Jazeera — Four charged over toppling of UK slave trader statue in Bristol

records.name: South Sea Company
records.scaleNote: Held the 1713 asiento allowing 4,800 captives a year to Spanish America for 30 years; actual deliveries fell far short, and the Church Commissioners' 2023 report cites c. 34,000 people transported, while other estimates are higher.
records.base: South Sea House, Threadneedle Street, London
aliases: The Governor and Company of the merchants of Great Britain, trading to the South Seas
records.origins: Founded in 1711 as a public–private scheme to consolidate British government debt in exchange for trading privileges in Spanish America.
records.role_summary: Under the Treaty of Utrecht (1713) it received the asiento, the contract to supply enslaved Africans to Spanish colonies, plus one annual trading ship. It bought captives (often from the Royal African Company and in Jamaica) and shipped them to ports such as Cartagena, Portobelo, Veracruz and Buenos Aires.

roleDetail.d: Contract for 4,800 enslaved people a year for 30 years, plus a 'navío de permiso' for general trade.
Historians disagree on whether the slave trade was profitable or mainly a cover for smuggling; disputes fed the 1739 War of Jenkins' Ear.
Speculation in its shares produced the South Sea Bubble crash of 1720.

records.legacy: The asiento was surrendered in 1750 and the company wound up in 1853. Its shareholders included Queen Anne's Bounty (Church of England), whose stake was the main basis of the Church Commissioners' 2023 £100m commitment.

legacyDetail.d: By 1777 Queen Anne's Bounty held £406,942 of South Sea stock, per the Church Commissioners' 2023 report.

sources.label: Wikipedia — South Sea Company
Britannica — Asiento de negros
University of Southampton — South Sea Company and the asiento (working paper)

records.name: Lascelles family (Earls of Harewood)
records.scaleNote: Edwin Lascelles at one point owned or managed 24 West Indian plantations with over 3,000 enslaved people (per Harewood House Trust); by 1787 the family held over 27,000 acres in Barbados, Jamaica, Grenada and Tobago (per University of York).
records.origins: A Yorkshire gentry family; Henry Lascelles (1690–1753) went to Barbados, became Collector of Customs, and built a fortune as a merchant, slave trader, government contractor and lender to planters.
records.role_summary: Combined slave trading, sugar shipping and plantation lending; foreclosures on indebted planters made them owners of many estates. Their profits built Harewood House (1759–71).

roleDetail.d: Henry Lascelles supplied enslaved Africans and credit to planters in Barbados; defaults brought plantations into the family.
Henry, 2nd Earl of Harewood, was awarded compensation, e.g. £6,486 for 292 people on Belle estate, Barbados (per LBS claim records).
Enslaved people on Lascelles plantations took part in Bussa's Rebellion in Barbados in 1816.

records.legacy: The family kept four Barbados plantations into the 20th century and sold its last Caribbean estate in 1975. Harewood House Trust now researches and presents this history, and David Lascelles co-founded the Heirs of Slavery group.

legacyDetail.d: Harewood has acknowledged that the house was built with slavery profits and runs school sessions on the trade.
David Lascelles, 8th Earl, co-founded the group with Laura Trevelyan.

sources.label: University of York — Harewood and slavery project
Harewood House Trust — Lascelles, slavery and the West Indies
UCL LBS — Henry Lascelles, 2nd Earl of Harewood
UCL LBS — Claim, Belle estate, Barbados

records.name: Beckford family
records.scaleNote: Among Jamaica's largest planter dynasties; William Thomas Beckford inherited (1770) about £1 million, Fonthill, and Jamaican plantations with about 3,000 enslaved people.
records.origins: Peter Beckford (c. 1643–1710) went to Jamaica in 1662, bought land and rose to acting governor. Later generations accumulated a large network of sugar estates.
records.role_summary: Owned and profited from Jamaican sugar plantations worked by enslaved people, as absentee owners after the move to England. Alderman William Beckford (1709–70) was MP and twice Lord Mayor of London (1762, 1769) and a leader of the West India interest.

roleDetail.d: Alderman Beckford used City of London office and Parliament to defend planter interests.
Enslaved people on his Esher estate in St Mary joined the 1760 uprising, which was crushed with mass executions.
His son spent the fortune on Fonthill Abbey and art collecting.

records.legacy: Fonthill Abbey's tower collapsed in 1825 after the fortune declined. A statue of Alderman Beckford still stands in London's Guildhall, and there have been calls to add context about the people he enslaved.

legacyDetail.d: Campaigners have argued that its inscription should acknowledge the 3,000 enslaved Africans behind the family's wealth.

sources.label: Wikipedia — William Beckford (politician)
National Gallery — William Thomas Beckford
National Trust for Scotland — William Beckford (1760–1844), part one

records.name: Hibbert family
records.scaleNote: Jamaica slave factors, planters and London West India merchants; one estimate puts family holdings at c. 900 enslaved people (figures vary by source).
records.origins: A Manchester merchant family; Thomas Hibbert settled in Kingston, Jamaica in the 1730s and became a leading factor selling newly arrived African captives to planters.
records.role_summary: Sold enslaved Africans in Jamaica, owned plantations, and ran the London house that shipped sugar and supplies. George Hibbert (1757–1837) led the London pro-slavery lobby and the West India Dock Company.

roleDetail.d: Bought cargoes of captives from slave ships and resold them to planters.
George Hibbert, MP and London alderman, spoke against abolition of the slave trade (per LBS).
A founding director and chairman of the West India Dock Company (docks opened 1802).

records.legacy: The West India Docks now house the Museum of London Docklands, whose 'London, Sugar & Slavery' gallery and 'Slavery, Culture and Collecting' display examine George Hibbert. A later Robert Hibbert founded the Hibbert Trust, a theological charity.

legacyDetail.d: The Museum of London Docklands presents Hibbert as collector, philanthropist and enslaver.

sources.label: UCL LBS — George Hibbert
London Museum — Portrait of George Hibbert
Museum of London Docklands — Slavery, Culture and Collecting

records.name: Gladstone family (Sir John Gladstone)
records.scaleNote: Per LBS, Sir John Gladstone owned or held mortgages over 2,508 enslaved people in British Guiana and Jamaica and received c. £106,769 compensation, among the largest awards to any individual.
records.origins: Born in Leith, John Gladstone made a fortune in Liverpool trading Calcutta goods, Virginia tobacco and American grain. From 1803 he bought sugar estates in Demerara, including Vreedenhoop (1826, 430 enslaved people).
records.role_summary: Absentee owner of plantations in British Guiana and Jamaica and a leading defender of slavery in Parliament and the press. After emancipation he pioneered shipping indentured labourers from India to his Guiana estates (1838).

roleDetail.d: The 1823 Demerara uprising began on his Success plantation; its violent suppression shaped the abolition debate.
Received c. £106,769 in 1830s compensation (per LBS), including c. £15,052 for 806 people in Jamaica.
Organised the first shipment of Indian indentured labourers to British Guiana.

records.legacy: His son William Ewart Gladstone became Liberal prime minister; family wealth endowed institutions such as Gladstone's Library. In August 2023 descendants apologised in Guyana and pledged c. £100,000 toward a University of Guyana institute; Guyanese critics called it insufficient.

legacyDetail.d: Charles Gladstone read the apology at the University of Guyana on 25 August 2023.
President Irfaan Ali did not attend and called for state reparations.

sources.label: UCL LBS — John Gladstone
AP via WSLS — Descendants of a British owner of slaves in Guyana apologize
ITV News — William Gladstone's descendants to apologise

records.name: Codrington family
records.scaleNote: Held Betty's Hope and other Antigua estates and leased Barbuda for generations; per LBS, Betty's Hope held 380 enslaved people in 1817 and Clare Hall's 1835 award was £4,442 for 296 people.
records.origins: Christopher Codrington the elder moved from Barbados to Antigua and founded Betty's Hope in the 1670s. His son Christopher (1668–1710) was Governor of the Leeward Islands and a fellow of All Souls, Oxford.
records.role_summary: Ran sugar plantations on Antigua and Barbados and leased Barbuda, enslaving thousands over two centuries. Christopher Codrington's 1710 will left two Barbados plantations, with their enslaved workers, to the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel, and £10,000 to All Souls for a library.

roleDetail.d: Left the Barbados estates to the SPG (Church of England missionary society) and £10,000 to All Souls College.
Christopher Bethell Codrington was a Tory MP for Tewkesbury (1797–1812) who opposed abolition of the slave trade (per LBS).

records.legacy: In 2020 All Souls stopped calling its library the Codrington Library, added a memorial plaque, and pledged £100,000 to Codrington College, Barbados, but kept his statue. Barbuda's main town is still named Codrington.

legacyDetail.d: The college made 'plain its abhorrence of slavery' but critics say the statue should go.

sources.label: UCL LBS — Claim, Clare Hall, Antigua
All Souls College — All Souls College and the Codrington legacy
Wikipedia — Codrington Plantations

records.name: Trevelyan family
records.scaleNote: Owned c. 1,000 enslaved people on six Grenada plantations and received c. £34,000 compensation in the 1830s (c. £3m today), per family statements and press reports.
records.origins: An English gentry family of baronets and later public servants and historians. Grenada became British in 1763; the exact date the family acquired its estates is not confirmed here.
records.role_summary: Absentee owners of sugar plantations in Grenada worked by enslaved Africans, compensated when slavery ended. They are now best known for their descendants' 2023 apology.

roleDetail.d: Six plantations with c. 1,000 enslaved people.
c. £34,000 awarded in the 1830s under the 1833 Act.

records.legacy: On 27 February 2023 former BBC journalist Laura Trevelyan and relatives apologised in Grenada and gave £100,000 toward a community fund; the Grenada National Reparations Commission welcomed it. She co-founded Heirs of Slavery with David Lascelles.

legacyDetail.d: A letter signed by seven family members called slavery a crime against humanity.
Family member John Dower urged the UK government to negotiate with CARICOM.

sources.label: APPG on Afrikan Reparations — British slave owners' family issue public apology in Grenada
Inverness Courier (PA) — Family descended from slaveowners to apologise and pay £100,000 to Grenada
Antigua Observer — Trevelyan family's slavery apology seen as significant move

records.name: Richard Oswald
records.scaleNote: Lead partner of Grant, Oswald & Co., which ran Bunce Island, the largest British slave fort on the Upper Guinea 'Rice Coast'; it shipped thousands of captives, many to South Carolina rice planters.
records.origins: A Scottish merchant from Caithness who trained in Glasgow and became a wealthy London merchant and army contractor during the Seven Years' War.
records.role_summary: With Alexander Grant and partners he bought Bunce Island in 1748, rebuilt its fort, and made it a major slave-trading depot. Henry Laurens sold the firm's captives in Charleston on commission.

roleDetail.d: The partners rebuilt the fort, added a shipyard and expanded its African workforce.
Laurens took 10% commission on sales of Bunce Island captives in South Carolina.
He was Britain's chief negotiator for the 1782–83 Treaty of Paris, facing his former agent Laurens.

records.legacy: Oswald's Ayrshire estate, Auchincruive, was bought with trade profits. Bunce Island passed to his nephews the Andersons, is now a protected Sierra Leone heritage site, and is a focus for Gullah Geechee descendants in the US.

legacyDetail.d: The University of Edinburgh's Managing Imperial Legacies project examines his career.

sources.label: Wikipedia — Richard Oswald (merchant)
Yale Gilder Lehrman Center — Bunce Island history
University of Edinburgh — Richard Oswald and Bunce Island, Sierra Leone

records.name: Tarleton family
records.scaleNote: One of Liverpool's largest merchant houses; the Tarleton brothers had 39 ships registered in Liverpool between 1786 and 1804, many of them in the slave trade.
records.origins: John Tarleton (1718–73) built a fortune in the Caribbean sugar trade and slaving voyages, continuing earlier family trade with the West Indies and Africa. His sons John, Clayton and Thomas ran the family firm.
records.role_summary: Financed and dispatched slaving voyages from Liverpool and traded West India produce. The family dominated Liverpool politics in defence of the trade: Clayton was mayor (1792) and Banastre was MP for Liverpool (1790–1812).

roleDetail.d: 39 Liverpool-registered ships 1786–1804.
The cavalry commander of the American war was a vocal Commons defender of the slave trade, though he never joined the family business.

records.legacy: Family papers (1678–1838) document their slave-trade dealings. Banastre's portraits and Liverpool memorials have been re-examined since 2020.

legacyDetail.d: The University of Liverpool's Victoria Gallery revisited Banastre Tarleton's reputation in 2020.

sources.label: University of Liverpool Victoria Gallery & Museum — Hero to Zero
British Online Archives — Papers of the Tarleton family 1678–1838
Wikipedia — Banastre Tarleton

records.name: Earle family
records.scaleNote: Multi-generational Liverpool slave traders whose archive is the Merseyside Maritime Museum's largest on the trade; voyage totals are not given here.
records.origins: A Liverpool merchant family active from the early 18th century. Brothers William (1721–88) and Thomas Earle became prominent slave-ship owners and traders.
records.role_summary: Sent slaving voyages to the Bight of Biafra (Old Calabar), the Gold Coast and elsewhere. Through Livorno they imported Italian glass beads used as trade goods, and they supplied William Davenport.

roleDetail.d: A 1751 letter of instruction for a slaving voyage to Calabar survives, along with a letter to an African trader about two relatives taken 'in error'.
The Earles brought many of Davenport's bead cargoes from Livorno.

records.legacy: Sir George Earle donated the family papers to Merseyside Maritime Museum in 1993. They underpin research at the International Slavery Museum.

legacyDetail.d: Seventeen boxes covering the 1700s to the 1930s.

sources.label: National Museums Liverpool — Family and business papers of the Earle family
UCL LBS — William Earle
Historic Society of Lancashire and Cheshire — Littler, The Earle collection

records.name: William Davenport
records.scaleNote: Invested in about 160 slaving voyages in about 70 vessels (per National Museums Liverpool), carrying almost 40,000 Africans; by ships disembarked, possibly Liverpool's most prolific slave trader.
records.origins: Born in London, he was apprenticed to the Liverpool slave trader William Whaley, with whom he invested in eight voyages in 1748–53.
records.role_summary: Took shares in slaving voyages to the Cameroons, Old Calabar and elsewhere, and specialised in supplying trade goods, especially glass beads from Italy, Silesia and Bohemia, which made up a quarter to a half of some cargoes.

roleDetail.d: In the 1770s beads made up 25–50% of the value of his cargoes to the Cameroons.
Also dealt in ivory, sugar, coffee and tobacco.

records.legacy: His business archive at Merseyside Maritime Museum is one of the most complete records of an 18th-century slave-trading firm and a key source for historians such as David Richardson.

legacyDetail.d: Davenport & Co. papers (1745–97) include bead and cowrie account books.

sources.label: National Museums Liverpool — Archives of William Davenport (1725–1797)
Gresham College — Liverpool and the slave trade
Wikipedia — William Davenport (slave trader)

records.name: Thomas Leyland
records.scaleNote: Helped finance about 69–72 slaving voyages carrying c. 22,000 Africans (per HSBC History and voyage-database research); left c. £600,000 in 1827.
records.origins: A Liverpool merchant whose start-up capital reportedly came from a lottery win; he moved from general shipping into slaving voyages by 1783.
records.role_summary: Merchant and ship-owner who financed dozens of slaving voyages, then a banker whose firm Leyland & Bullins lent to other traders. As three-time mayor (first 1798) he presided while the council petitioned against regulation of the trade.

roleDetail.d: As merchant and ship-owner he helped finance 72 transatlantic voyages (per HSBC History).
Founded Leyland & Bullins (1807) with his nephew Richard Bullin.

records.legacy: Leyland & Bullins merged into what became Midland Bank and is now part of HSBC, which publishes its history. His letter books survive in the Liverpool Record Office.

legacyDetail.d: HSBC's own archive acknowledges Leyland's role in financing slave voyages.

sources.label: HSBC History — Leyland and Bullins
Wikipedia — Thomas Leyland
Myles Zhang — The Slave Trader Turned Banker (paper)

records.name: Heywood brothers (Arthur & Benjamin Heywood)
records.scaleNote: Liverpool slave-ship owners: Arthur and Benjamin Heywood invested in 82 slaving voyages, and with Benjamin's sons 133 voyages carrying an estimated 42,000 captives (c. 6,000 of whom died), per a University of Manchester Rylands study drawing on SlaveVoyages; their profits founded Heywood's Bank (1773), an ancestor of Barclays.
records.origins: Merchant brothers Arthur and Benjamin Heywood traded from Liverpool, including as co-owners of slaving ships. Benjamin later moved to Manchester and with his sons founded a separate bank there (1788), Heywood Brothers & Co, later part of the NatWest group's history.
records.role_summary: Owned and invested in slave ships, then used the capital to found a bank (c. 1773) that served Liverpool's Atlantic merchants.

roleDetail.d: Arthur, Benjamin and Benjamin's sons Benjamin Arthur and Nathaniel all co-owned slaving voyages.
Arthur Heywood's Liverpool bank was established by 1773.

records.legacy: The Liverpool bank was absorbed by the Bank of Liverpool (1883), later Martins Bank, which Barclays bought in 1969. The Martins Bank Building on Water Street, Liverpool, survives as a listed building.

legacyDetail.d: Heywood's → Bank of Liverpool → Martins → Barclays.

Wikipedia — Bank of Liverpool

records.name: John Bolton
records.scaleNote: Credited by the Transatlantic Slave Trade Database (via LBS) with 69 slaving voyages from 1788 to 1807, peaking at five or more ships a year from Liverpool in 1798–1805.
records.origins: Apprenticed in St Vincent in 1773, he worked in the Caribbean before returning to Liverpool around 1782–83 with £10,000 to start a merchant firm.
records.role_summary: One of the last great Liverpool slave traders, increasingly the sole owner of his ships. After 1807 he and Bolton & Littledale became leading cotton traders with British Guiana, where he also owned estates.

roleDetail.d: Operated right up to abolition of the trade in 1807.
His will refers to property in Demerara, St Vincent and St Croix.

records.legacy: He died worth c. £180,000 and left Storrs Hall on Windermere to a clergyman. He is documented in the LBS database.

legacyDetail.d: Storrs Hall, bought from slave-trade wealth, is now a hotel.

sources.label: UCL LBS — John Bolton

records.name: Sir John Tobin
records.scaleNote: Captain on 6 slaving voyages (1793–1803) and owner in 10 (1794–1804), per LBS; later a leading palm-oil importer.
records.origins: A Manx-born seaman who rose as a privateer and slave-ship captain before becoming a Liverpool merchant.
records.role_summary: Commanded and then owned slaving ships. After 1807 he turned his West African trade networks to palm oil, a shift that shaped Liverpool's 19th-century Africa trade.

roleDetail.d: Sailed as captain, then invested as owner in slaving voyages.
LBS says he was instrumental in converting slave-trade links into the palm-oil trade.

records.legacy: Mayor of Liverpool in 1819–20 and knighted in 1820. His career shows continuity between the slave trade and later 'legitimate' commerce with West Africa.

legacyDetail.d: Delta and Calabar trading relationships carried over from slaves to palm oil.

sources.label: UCL LBS — Sir John Tobin
National Museums Liverpool — Sir John Tobin
Wikipedia — Sir John Tobin

records.name: Pinney family (John Pretor Pinney)
records.scaleNote: 903 men, women and children are known to have lived enslaved on Mountravers, Nevis, 1680/81–1834 (per Bristol University research by Eickelmann & Small); Pinney & Tobin became a leading Bristol sugar house.
records.origins: John Pretor inherited the Nevis plantations in 1762 from a distant cousin on condition that he take the name Pinney. He lived on Nevis managing Mountravers until the 1780s.
records.role_summary: Ran a sugar plantation on Nevis worked by enslaved people, then moved to Bristol as a West India merchant and lender to planters. He brought enslaved servants, including Pero Jones and Fanny Coker, to his Bristol house.

roleDetail.d: Mountravers, also called Pinney's Estate, Nevis.
Profits built the Great George Street house (c. 1790) and a sugar business.
Pero Jones, bought as a child, lived and worked in the house; Pero's Bridge is named after him.

records.legacy: The house is now Bristol's Georgian House Museum, whose displays were revised in 2018 to list the 903 people enslaved on Mountravers. It is Grade II* listed partly for this connection.

legacyDetail.d: Long marketed as a 'West India merchant's house', it now centres the enslaved.

sources.label: Wikipedia — John Pinney

records.name: Barclays
records.scaleNote: Not a slave trader itself, but descends from banks founded with slave-trade capital (Heywood's, Liverpool) and its founding Barclay partners financed West India trade and plantation mortgages.
records.origins: Grew from a Quaker goldsmith-banking partnership in Lombard Street, London (1690s). Through 20th-century mergers it absorbed many regional banks.
records.role_summary: Predecessor banks lent to slave traders and planters: Heywood's Bank was founded by Liverpool slave-ship owners, and the Barclay family's business financed tobacco and West India trade. David Barclay acquired Unity Valley Pen in Jamaica through a debt and in 1795 freed and resettled 30 enslaved people in Philadelphia.

roleDetail.d: Heywood's → Bank of Liverpool (1883) → Martins → Barclays (1969).
Barclays' archive highlights David Barclay's manumission; the LRB argues this framing is selective.

records.legacy: Barclays has said it may have benefited from the slave trade through acquired banks (2007) and in 2020 published archive material on Unity Valley; critics say it has not fully reckoned with its history.

legacyDetail.d: Historian Christopher L. Brown called the bank's statement 'selective, misleading'.

sources.label: Barclays — From the archives: October's freedom from slavery
London Review of Books — Christopher L. Brown, Funhouse Mirror
Wikipedia — Heywood's Bank
UCL LBS — Person freed from Unity Valley by David Barclay

records.name: Lloyd's of London
records.scaleNote: Lloyd's says it was the global centre for insuring Britain's shipping industry, which carried an estimated 3.2 million enslaved Africans (1640–early 1800s).
records.origins: Began in Edward Lloyd's coffee house (from 1688) where merchants and ship-owners met to arrange marine insurance; the 1771 subscribers formalised the market.
records.role_summary: Underwriters in the Lloyd's market insured slave ships, their cargoes and the enslaved people aboard as property. Several founding subscribers were slave traders or slave-owners.

roleDetail.d: Policies covered ships and captives as cargo, with 'perils of the sea' and insurrection clauses.
Founding subscriber Simon Fraser held at least 162 enslaved people and received compensation for a Dominica plantation.
Lloyd's research found John Julius Angerstein was not a slave trader but benefited through marine insurance; it dropped calling him 'Father of Lloyd's'.

records.legacy: In June 2020 Lloyd's apologised for its 'shameful' role and pledged funding for Black and ethnic-minority causes, and later published research on its 1771 founders with Lancaster University's William Pettigrew.

legacyDetail.d: Issued alongside Greene King after LBS database coverage.

sources.label: Lloyd's — 1771 founders (Transatlantic slave trade research)
Lloyd's — John Julius Angerstein history report
Insurance Business — Lloyd's of London apologises over founders' slavery links

records.name: Bank of England
records.scaleNote: Owned two Grenada plantations and 599 enslaved people in the late 1780s after a 1772 £160,000 loan defaulted; LBS-based press analyses in 2020 counted at least 11 former governors and 16 early directors (c. 25–27 people) with slavery links.
aliases: The Old Lady of Threadneedle Street
records.origins: Founded in 1694 as banker to the English government. Its directors and governors came from the City merchant elite, including West India merchants and slave-owners.
records.role_summary: Lent £160,000 in 1772 against the Bacolet and Chemin plantations in Grenada, took sole possession in the late 1780s with 599 enslaved people, and sold them in 1790. Former governors such as Jeremiah Harman and Benjamin Buck Greene had slavery-derived wealth.

roleDetail.d: A 1788 inventory names the 599 enslaved women, men and children the Bank owned.
Estimates differ: at least 11 governors and 16 directors (Guardian/LBS, 2020), 25 governors and directors (City AM), up to 44 associated individuals (Positive Money).

records.legacy: In June 2020 the Bank apologised for 'inexcusable' links of former governors and directors and removed their portraits. Its museum ran the 'Slavery & the Bank' exhibition (2022–24).

legacyDetail.d: Campaigners argue acknowledgement has not been matched by action.

sources.label: Bank of England Museum — A Story of Archival Discovery: The Bank and the Grenada Plantations
Bank of England Museum — Beginning the exhibition: Slavery & the Bank
CNN — Bank of England apologizes for slave trade links
Positive Money — Slavery & the Bank: acknowledgement is not action

records.name: N M Rothschild & Sons
records.scaleNote: Nathan Mayer Rothschild, with Moses Montefiore and a consortium, was contractor for the 1835 'West India loan', raised by selling government consols and annuities, which funded the greater part (c. £15m) of the £20 million paid to slave-owners; it was not a slave-trading firm.
records.base: New Court, St Swithin's Lane, London
records.origins: Founded in London by Nathan Mayer Rothschild (1777–1836) in the early 19th century; it became a leading arranger of British government loans.
records.role_summary: Led the consortium that took up the 1835 'West India loan' the Treasury used to pay slave-owners compensation under the 1833 Act. The Rothschild Archive presents Nathan's role as supporting abolition by financing the compensation that made it possible.

roleDetail.d: Arranged with Moses Montefiore; the remaining c. £5m came from other Treasury funds.
2009 Financial Times research reported that Nathan Mayer Rothschild had taken enslaved people in Antigua as loan collateral; the firm said it 'greatly regrets' any link.
Whether the loan is seen as aiding abolition or rewarding slave-owners is a matter of interpretation; the money went to owners, not the enslaved.

records.legacy: The successor Rothschild & Co still operates. The 1835 borrowing was later folded into other government stock; a February 2018 HM Treasury tweet (later deleted) said it was finally paid off in 2015, though Full Fact notes that how much of the original debt was still outstanding by then is unknown.

legacyDetail.d: Issued alongside law firm Freshfields after FT research.

sources.label: The Rothschild Archive — Guide to the Archive: The West India loan
Reuters via Investing.com — UK law firm and bank regret slave trade links
Business & Human Rights Resource Centre — Businesses regret links with slavery
Full Fact — What we know about the government loan to pay slave owners compensation

records.name: Greene King (Benjamin Greene)
records.scaleNote: Founder Benjamin Greene (1780–1860) owned estates in St Kitts and Montserrat and was awarded £4,033 15s 7d compensation for 231 enslaved people (per LBS; the Telegraph put it at c. £500,000 today).
records.origins: Benjamin Greene, a former Whitbread apprentice, founded the Bury St Edmunds brewery in 1799 and acquired West India estates, which his son Benjamin Buck Greene managed from 1829.
records.role_summary: Greene owned plantations worked by enslaved people, used his newspaper to oppose abolition, and claimed compensation in the 1830s. The family firm Blyth & Greene later became a major colonial shipping house.

roleDetail.d: Greene King's 2020 statement called his profiting from slavery and opposition to abolition 'inexcusable'.
Son Benjamin Buck Greene was Bank of England governor 1873–75 (per LBS).

records.legacy: Greene King, now one of Britain's largest pub and brewing groups, apologised in June 2020 and pledged investment in BAME communities. The brewery was run by another son, Edward Greene.

legacyDetail.d: Made the same day as Lloyd's of London, prompted by the LBS database.

sources.label: ITV News — Greene King and Lloyd's of London apologise for slavery links
UCL News — Opinion: The slavery business contributed to the building of modern Britain
UCL LBS — Benjamin Buck Greene
UCL LBS — Benjamin Greene (1780–1860)

records.name: Slavery Abolition Act 1833 & £20m compensation
records.description: Act ending slavery in most British colonies from 1 August 1834, replaced by 'apprenticeship' until 1838. Parliament voted £20 million (c. 40% of annual government spending) to compensate slave-owners; the enslaved received nothing. Payments went to some 40,000+ claimants listed in the LBS database.

records.name: Slave Compensation Commission
records.description: Body that met from October 1833 to adjudicate and distribute the £20 million, using colonial slave registers; payments were made by the National Debt Office (1835–43). Its records (T 71, NDO 4) at The National Archives underpin the UCL LBS database.

records.name: 1835 £15m compensation loan
records.description: £15 million raised in 1835 by a syndicate led by Nathan Mayer Rothschild and Moses Montefiore (the 'West India loan'), funding most of the £20 million compensation to slave-owners; the other £5 million was paid directly in government stock. The debt was later merged into other gilts and finally redeemed in 2015 during government debt restructuring, as a since-deleted February 2018 HM Treasury tweet publicised; Full Fact notes that how much of the original sum remained outstanding by 2015 is unknown.

records.name: Port of Liverpool
records.description: Overtook London and Bristol by the 1740s and by 1750 sent more slaving voyages than both combined; in 1793–1807 it accounted for roughly 80–85% of British slaving voyages. Liverpool ships carried an estimated well over 1 million Africans before 1807.

records.name: Port of Bristol
records.description: Britain's leading slaving port in the 1730s–40s (c. 38% of British voyages in 1739–48), with an estimated 2,000+ slaving voyages overall carrying around half a million Africans. Its sugar and tobacco trade funded much of Georgian Bristol.

records.name: Port of London
records.description: Base of the Royal African and South Sea companies and England's leading slaving port until the 1720s; it remained the financial, insurance and sugar-importing centre of the slavery economy. Robert Milligan's statue at West India Quay was removed in June 2020.

records.name: Bunce Island
records.description: Island fort in the Sierra Leone River, used by the RAC and from 1748 by Grant, Oswald & Co., which made it the largest British slave castle on the Rice Coast. Many captives went to South Carolina and Georgia rice plantations via Henry Laurens; it later passed to Oswald's nephews, the Andersons.

records.name: Cape Coast Castle
records.description: Built as a Swedish lodge (c. 1653) on the Gold Coast, captured by the English in 1664, and expanded by the RAC as its West African headquarters. Captives were held in windowless dungeons before passing the 'Door of No Return'; it was the seat of British Gold Coast administration until 1877 and became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979.

records.name: Church of England (SPG & Queen Anne's Bounty)
records.description: Through the Society for the Propagation of the Gospel the Church owned the Codrington plantations in Barbados from 1710, and Queen Anne's Bounty (est. 1704) invested heavily in the South Sea Company. Its 2023 report led the Church Commissioners to pledge £100m; Archbishop Justin Welby said he was 'deeply sorry'.

records.name: Codrington Plantations, Barbados
records.description: Two sugar estates left to the SPG by Christopher Codrington in 1710, worked by enslaved people whom the Society owned; for a period they were branded with the word 'Society'. USPG ended its stewardship in 1983 and has apologised; Codrington College still stands on the land.

records.name: Company of Royal Adventurers into Africa
records.description: Chartered December 1660 under the Duke of York and Prince Rupert, first for gold; its 1663 charter explicitly added the slave trade. War with the Dutch and losses ruined it by 1667, and it was replaced by the Royal African Company in 1672.

records.name: Company of Merchants Trading to Africa
records.description: Regulated company created by Parliament in 1750 to take over the RAC's forts from 1752, funded by annual parliamentary grants; any British merchant could join. It ran Cape Coast Castle and other forts until abolished in 1821, when the Crown took over.

records.name: Jesus of Lübeck
records.description: A 700-ton Hanseatic-built warship bought by Henry VIII and lent by Elizabeth I to John Hawkins for his 1564 and 1567 slaving voyages. It was abandoned to the Spanish at San Juan de Ulúa in 1568.

records.name: Heywood's Bank (Liverpool)
records.description: Bank founded in Liverpool by slave-trading merchant Arthur Heywood and his brother, established by 1773. Bought by the Bank of Liverpool in 1883, which became Martins Bank, acquired by Barclays in 1969.

records.name: Leyland & Bullins
records.description: Liverpool bank opened in 1807 by slave trader Thomas Leyland and his nephew Richard Bullin, which lent to other slave traders. It later passed by amalgamation into Midland Bank, now HSBC.

records.name: West India Docks, London
records.description: Secure docks on the Isle of Dogs, opened 1802 and promoted by West India merchants such as George Hibbert and Robert Milligan, to handle slave-grown sugar, rum and coffee. Its surviving warehouse houses the Museum of London Docklands and its 'London, Sugar & Slavery' gallery.

records.name: Harewood House
records.description: Country house near Leeds built 1759–71 by Edwin Lascelles with wealth from Caribbean sugar and slavery. The Harewood House Trust now researches and openly presents the estate's slavery history.

records.name: Georgian House Museum, Bristol
records.description: John Pinney's c. 1790 town house on Great George Street, a museum since 1939. Displays revised in 2018 tell the story of the Nevis plantation and the enslaved servant Pero Jones.

records.name: Mountravers plantation, Nevis
records.description: Pinney family sugar plantation on Nevis; research has identified 903 enslaved men, women and children who lived there between 1680/81 and 1834.

records.name: Statue of Edward Colston (Bristol)
records.description: Bronze statue erected in 1895, toppled by protesters on 7 June 2020 and rolled into Bristol Harbour. Recovered by the council, it is now shown lying down and graffitied in the M Shed museum.

records.name: Bacolet & Chemin plantations, Grenada
records.description: Two Grenada sugar estates mortgaged to the Bank of England for £160,000 in 1772; after default the Bank took sole possession in the late 1780s with 599 named enslaved people, then sold them to James Baillie for £100,000 in 1790.

records.name: Church Commissioners' £100m fund (2023)
records.description: In January 2023 the Church Commissioners committed £100m over nine years to impact investment, research and grants after finding Queen Anne's Bounty's slavery links; the Church avoids the word 'reparations' because no individuals are paid.

records.name: UCL Legacies of British Slavery database
records.description: University College London project (begun 2009) that put online the identities of all 40,000+ slave-owners in the British Caribbean, Mauritius and the Cape at abolition, from compensation records. Its findings prompted the 2020 apologies by Lloyd's, Greene King and the Bank of England.

records.name: All Souls College Library (formerly 'Codrington Library')
records.description: Oxford library built 1716–20 with Christopher Codrington's £10,000 bequest. In 2020 the college stopped using his name, added a memorial plaque to the enslaved and pledged £100,000 to Codrington College, Barbados, but kept his statue.

records.name: Heirs of Slavery
records.description: Group of descendants of British slave-owners, co-founded by Laura Trevelyan and David Lascelles, that encourages apology and reparative justice and supports CARICOM's reparations call.

records.name: Slave Trade Act 1807
records.description: Act of Parliament banning British subjects from the Atlantic slave trade from 1 May 1807 (slavery itself continued until 1834–38). Liverpool's merchants and MPs such as Banastre Tarleton had fought it.

records.name: International Slavery Museum, Liverpool
records.description: National Museums Liverpool museum at the Albert Dock, opened in 2007 for the bicentenary of the 1807 Act. With the Merseyside Maritime Museum archive it holds the Earle and Davenport papers.

events.title: Hawkins's first English slaving voyage
events.text: John Hawkins took c. 300 Africans from the Sierra Leone coast and sold them in Spanish Hispaniola, beginning England's transatlantic slave trade.

events.title: Elizabeth I invests in slaving
events.text: The Queen lent the royal ship Jesus of Lübeck to Hawkins's second slaving voyage.

events.title: Defeat at San Juan de Ulúa
events.text: A Spanish fleet attacked Hawkins's third slaving expedition in Mexico; Hawkins and Drake escaped but most ships were lost.

events.title: Company of Royal Adventurers chartered
events.text: Charles II chartered the company under the Duke of York; its 1663 charter explicitly included the slave trade.

events.title: Royal African Company founded
events.text: The RAC received a monopoly of English trade to West Africa and became the largest single shipper of enslaved Africans in the trade's history.

source.label: PBS Africans in America — The Royal African Company

events.title: Slave trade opened to all English merchants
events.text: Parliament ended the RAC monopoly, letting private traders from Bristol and later Liverpool expand the trade.

source.label: Schools History — Lifting of the Royal African Company monopoly

events.title: Codrington bequest to the Church
events.text: Christopher Codrington left two Barbados plantations and their enslaved workers to the SPG, and £10,000 to All Souls College.

source.label: All Souls College — The Codrington legacy

events.title: Britain wins the asiento
events.text: Under the Treaty of Utrecht, the South Sea Company gained the contract to supply 4,800 enslaved Africans a year to Spanish America for 30 years.

events.title: Grant, Oswald & Co. buys Bunce Island
events.text: Richard Oswald's London firm took over the Sierra Leone fort, shipping captives to Charleston via Henry Laurens.

source.label: Yale Gilder Lehrman Center — Bunce Island history

events.title: Bank of England's Grenada loan
events.text: The Bank lent £160,000 on two Grenada plantations; after default it came to own 599 enslaved people, selling them in 1790.

source.label: Bank of England Museum — A Story of Archival Discovery

events.title: Demerara uprising begins on Gladstone estate
events.text: The large 1823 rebellion of enslaved people in Demerara began on John Gladstone's Success plantation and was violently suppressed.

source.label: AP via WSLS — Descendants of a British owner of slaves in Guyana apologize

events.title: Abolition Act and £20m compensation
events.text: Parliament abolished colonial slavery from 1834 and voted £20 million to slave-owners, distributed by the Slave Compensation Commission; the 1835 £15m loan arranged by N M Rothschild and Moses Montefiore funded most of it.

source.label: The National Archives — Office of Registry of Colonial Slaves and Slave Compensation Commission records

events.title: Compensation borrowing finally repaid
events.text: The last gilts into which the 1835 compensation borrowing had been consolidated were redeemed in 2015; a February 2018 HM Treasury tweet presenting this as a 'fact' drew criticism and was deleted. How much of the original debt was still outstanding is unknown (Full Fact).

source.label: Full Fact — What we know about the government loan to pay slave owners compensation

events.title: Colston statue toppled; corporate apologies
events.text: Protesters toppled Edward Colston's statue in Bristol on 7 June; within days Lloyd's of London, Greene King and the Bank of England apologised for historic slavery links.

events.title: Church fund and family apologies
events.text: The Church Commissioners pledged £100m (January); the Trevelyan family apologised in Grenada (February) and the Gladstone family in Guyana (August).

source.label: Civil Society — Church Commissioners pledges £100m to atone for links to chattel slavery
